document.abstract: Through the combination of digital TV and digital networking technologies, the transport of professional broadcast services is undergoing a tremendous evolution. After a move from analog to digital, specialized leased lines are being replaced progressively by powerful general purpose asynchronous transfer mode (ATM)-based networks. The most critical issue for the adoption of this new technology by the broadcast industry is the transport of live realtime broadcast services, for which the most serious constraints appear. The level of performance that can be expected for this application is a key point for the end-user broadcaster. After reviewing various elements of the ATM technology, this paper focuses on performance aspects: the mechanisms put in place, leading to commitments by both the end-user broadcaster and the network operator to a given level of performance are explained; practical performance results are given; and examples of large-scale deployments are described.

authors.bio: Jean Chatel received an engineering degree from ESEO (Ecole Supérieure d'Electonique de l'Ouest) and a doctorate from the University of Rennes, France. He joined CCETT in 1974 to work on the early developments of digital television for studio applications. — For 15 years Chatel has been with Thomson, particularly in charge of development of realtime digital television and HDTV signals processing systems, including studio systems, motion compensated standards conversion, and compression systems. His current position is marketing manager, advanced technology, dealing with compression and networking technology. Chatel is a SMPTE Fellow.

authors.bio: David Mouen Makoua received a degree in electrical engineering from INPG/ENSERG France in 1984. — He spent ten years in Thomson-CSF as senior engineer and was involved in military networking issues, mainly ATM equipment architecture. — Mouen joined Thomson Broadcast Systems in 1999 and is presently product manager for the network adaptor family, which addresses the delivery of high-quality audio/video over broadband telecom networks. He serves also as internal consultant for networking architecture issues.
authors.name: David Mouen Makoua

authors.bio: Laurent Thehault received an engineering degree from Supelec (Ecole Supérieure d'Electricité, France) in 1989. He joined the Thomson group in 1990, where he currently manages the development of network adaptor and service multiplexer. — While at Thomson, Laurent has worked on the design of high-rate serial interfaces and switches for audio and video, and ATM-based multiplexing and transport systems. Currently he is involved in quality-of-service issues for the transport of high-quality video over emerging high-bandwidth IP networks.
